indexPrompt.viz-one-slow-request: You time 20 requests to a model server, in milliseconds, and want to see how the times are spread. Most of them sit between 12 and 48 ms, and one takes 412 ms. You plot them with a histogram of 10 bins.
indexPrompt.viz-two-logging-rates: A training run lasts 2,000 steps. It records the training loss every 50 steps, at steps 50, 100, and so on to 2000, into the list train_log, and the validation loss every 200 steps, at steps 200, 400, and so on to 2000, into val_log. Both lists go on one plot against their position in the list rather than against the step they were recorded at.
indexPrompt.viz-a-band-on-a-log-axis: You train a model with 4 seeds on a hard problem and plot the mean validation loss with a band from one standard deviation below the mean to one above, on a log y axis because the loss falls by several factors of ten. At the last epoch the four runs end at 0.01, 0.1, 0.1 and 1.0. Use the standard deviation that divides by the number of runs, as np.std does.
indexPrompt.viz-overlapping-bands-paired-seeds: Two models are trained with the same 5 random seeds, so each seed gives both models the same data split and the same initial weights. A teammate plots each model's mean test accuracy with a band of one standard deviation, sees the two bands overlap, and concludes that neither model is better than the other.
indexPrompt.viz-box-plot-of-review-lengths: A shop compares how long its customers' reviews are in each product category with a box plot of word counts. The garden category has 9 reviews, from 38 to 104 words, and seaborn takes the box edges from NumPy's default percentile rule.
indexPrompt.viz-annotations-transposed: A classifier sorts 150 scanned documents into invoices, receipts and contracts, and its confusion matrix is drawn with imshow, the true classes as rows, and a count written into every cell. The counts are labelled with a loop that calls ax.text(i, j, ...), so a reader who reads a count off the figure may not be reading the cell they think they are.
indexPrompt.viz-data-needed-from-a-log-log-plot: You train the same model on 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, ..., 64,000 examples and plot its test error against the training set size $N$ with ax.loglog(N, err). The seven points fall on a straight line, from an error of 0.32 at $N = 1{,}000$ to 0.04 at $N = 64{,}000$.
